subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 3 · The Two Bridges — Leadership Behaviour and Motivation

questions.stem: Describe the autocratic leadership style from the Iowa studies.
options: The leader makes the decisions, tells employees what to do and closely supervises
The leader encourages participation in decisions and does not closely supervise the work
The leader does nothing and leaves employees to organise the work entirely for themselves
The leader only sets the goals and lets the team decide how and when to reach them
questions.why: Fast and clear, but produces dependence. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Identify what the democratic style produces, according to the chapter.
options: Commitment, better decisions on complex problems, and effort that continues without the leader
Fast decisions and clear direction, but followers who depend on the leader for every step and stop when the leader leaves
Confusion about who decides, because every member of the team expects to be consulted
Lower quality, because the people consulted know less about the problem than the leader
questions.why: Slower, but commitment. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Explain what the behavioural paradigm added to leadership.
options: It made leadership learnable — behaviour can be taught where traits cannot
It found the one best style that works in every situation and with every follower
It proved that leaders are born, because only certain people adopt the right behaviours
It replaced motivation theory, because behaviour explains performance without reference to needs
questions.why: But no single best style was found. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Identify the finding that produced the contingency paradigm.
options: Forty years of research found no single best style for all situations
Autocratic leadership is always best, because it produces results fastest
Democratic leadership is always best, because it produces the most commitment
Traits predict everything, so the leader's behaviour makes no difference
questions.why: The finding that produced Chapter 4. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Describe how the Michigan studies placed job-centred and employee-centred behaviour.
options: At two ends of one line — more of one means less of the other
As two independent dimensions that a leader can be high or low on at the same time
As the same thing described from the leader's and the follower's points of view
As five grid styles ranging from impoverished to team leader
questions.why: Michigan: one continuum. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Identify Ohio State's two dimensions.
options: Initiating structure and consideration
Need for power and need for affiliation
Autocratic and democratic behaviour
Task focus and time management
questions.why: Two independent dimensions. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Describe the 'high-high' leader.
options: High on initiating structure and high on consideration at once — the style later research favours
High on task behaviour only, with little attention to how the followers feel about the work or the leader
High on people behaviour only, with little attention to structuring the work
Low on both dimensions, leaving followers to organise the work themselves
questions.why: Ohio State showed you can do both. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Explain why the Ohio State finding matters.
options: Michigan says choose; Ohio State says you can do both — the basis of the Grid, Situational Leadership and the transformational leader
It proved Michigan right by showing that leaders who tried to do both ended up doing neither well
It ended behavioural research, because the two dimensions explained everything that needed explaining
It found the traits that produce each behaviour, linking the trait and behavioural paradigms
questions.why: Why it matters. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Identify the five Leadership Grid styles.
options: 1,1 impoverished; 9,1 authority-compliance; 1,9 country club; 5,5 middle of the road; 9,9 team leader
Autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire, servant and charismatic
Task leader, people leader, balanced leader, absent leader, complete team leader and crisis leader
Theory X, Theory Y, Theory Z, high-high and low-low
questions.why: Blake and Mouton. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Describe the 9,1 authority-compliance style.
options: Gets the job done; people are instruments — output with turnover and resentment
Keeps people happy and avoids pushing them, so deadlines slip while morale stays high
Minimum effort for either production or people, just enough to keep the job
High standards and commitment through trust, with both production and people high

questions.stem: Identify the Grid's ideal style and its two concerns.
options: 9,9 team leader — high concern for production and high concern for people
1,9 country club — high concern for people and low concern for production
5,5 middle of the road — moderate concern for both production and people
9,1 authority-compliance — high concern for production and low concern for people
questions.why: The textbook's ideal. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's caution about the 9,9 style.
options: Research is mixed — it is not best in every situation, but it is the best default
It is always best, whatever the situation, the followers or the task
It never works in practice, because nobody can sustain a high concern for both production and people at once
It is only for small teams, where the leader knows every follower personally
questions.why: Not a universal law. See §3.3.

questions.stem: Describe the motivation process in order.
options: Need → motive → behaviour → consequence → satisfaction or dissatisfaction
Behaviour → need → reward → satisfaction → new behaviour → new reward → habit
Goal → effort → performance → pay → satisfaction → higher goal
Consequence → need → motive → behaviour → reward
questions.why: The motivation process. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three classes of motivation theory.
options: Content, process and reinforcement
Trait, behaviour and contingency
Maslow, Herzberg and McClelland
Equity, expectancy and goal-setting
questions.why: Grouped by the question each answers. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Describe the question content theories answer.
options: WHAT motivates people — which needs
HOW people choose one behaviour over another
HOW consequences shape future behaviour
WHO emerges as the leader of the group
questions.why: Content theories. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Explain why leaders must know all three classes.
options: Content tells you which need is unmet; process tells you why the person is not trying; reinforcement tells you what your own behaviour is teaching them
Only one class is ever true for a given follower, so the leader must find which class fits each person
Exams require it, because the textbook covers all three classes and tests each of them
Each class is for a different industry — content for services, process for manufacturing, reinforcement for sales
questions.why: Why leaders must know all three. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Identify Maslow's five levels in order.
options: Physiological, safety, belongingness, esteem, self-actualisation
Pay, security, teamwork, praise, personal growth
Safety, physiological, esteem, belongingness, self-actualisation
Achievement, power, affiliation, esteem, safety
questions.why: Met lower first. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Describe Herzberg's maintenance factors.
options: Pay, conditions, security, policies — they prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate
Achievement and recognition — they create satisfaction but their absence does not cause dissatisfaction
Needs for power and affiliation — they must be maintained at a moderate level
Goals and feedback — they maintain performance once motivation has been established
questions.why: Fix maintenance first; then add motivators. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Identify Herzberg's motivator factors.
options: Achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth, the work itself
Pay, working conditions, job security, supervision and company policies
Rules, supervision, procedures and performance reviews
Bonuses, penalties, promotions and demotions
questions.why: Motivator factors create satisfaction. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Describe the leader's use of McClelland's acquired needs.
options: Give achievers challenge and feedback, power-seekers responsibility, affiliators teamwork
Pay everyone the same so that no need is favoured over another
Supervise everyone closely so that every need is met in exactly the same way for every follower
Give everyone a bonus, because money satisfies all three needs
questions.why: Applied to followers. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Describe equity theory.
options: People compare their inputs and outputs with others'; perceived inequity changes behaviour
Motivation equals expectancy times instrumentality times valence
Specific, difficult goals motivate more than vague or easy ones
Behaviour that is rewarded is repeated and behaviour that is not rewarded gradually fades away
questions.why: Adams. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Identify the three parts of expectancy theory.
options: Expectancy (can I do it?), instrumentality (will performance be rewarded?), valence (do I value the reward?)
Need (what is missing?), motive (why act?), behaviour (what is done?)
Input (what I give), output (what I get), comparison (what others get)
Goal (what is asked?), feedback (how am I doing?), acceptance (do I agree?)
questions.why: If any is near zero, so is effort. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Describe goal-setting theory.
options: Specific, difficult but achievable goals motivate more than vague or easy ones — when accepted and with feedback
Easy goals motivate most, because people enjoy the feeling of reaching them
Vague goals leave room for people to decide how to contribute
Goals do not matter, because motivation comes from the leader's behaviour
questions.why: Locke. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Identify the textbook format for writing an objective.
options: To + action verb + specific, measurable, single result + target date
Improve customer service across the department during the coming year
Do your best to serve customers well and let me know how it goes
Try harder next quarter so that the numbers look better for the review
questions.why: A goal you cannot measure cannot motivate. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four types of reinforcement.
options: Positive reinforcement, avoidance, extinction, punishment
Content, process, goal-setting, equity, expectancy and reinforcement
Praise, pay, promotion, perks and penalties
Maintenance, motivator, need and drive
questions.why: Skinner, as used in the textbook. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Describe extinction.
options: Withholding the reward so an unwanted behaviour fades — it also happens by accident when good work goes unnoticed
Giving something unpleasant after unwanted behaviour so that it is not repeated
Giving praise after good behaviour so that it is repeated more often
Behaving in a particular way in order to avoid a penalty or an unpleasant consequence
questions.why: Extinction. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Explain why variable schedules matter.
options: They produce the most durable behaviour — unpredictable recognition works; predictable annual bonuses stop motivating
They are cheaper, because the leader rewards less often than on a continuous schedule
They are easier to plan, because the leader does not have to reward every occurrence
They are required by law in most countries, which limit how often bonuses can be paid
questions.why: Schedules of reinforcement. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Identify the four steps of giving praise.
options: Tell exactly what was done correctly; tell why it matters; pause; encourage repeat performance
Say 'good job'; smile; move on to the next task; email HR a note for the file
Praise in public; criticise in public; repeat the message weekly; reward with a bonus at the end of the quarter
Pay the bonus; praise the person; promote them; pause before the next review
questions.why: Under a minute; costs nothing. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Identify the first step in the leader's diagnosis sequence.
options: Is a basic or maintenance need unmet — pay late, unsafe, insecure? Fix it first
Are the goals specific, measurable and accepted by the person?
What am I reinforcing by what I notice and reward?
Is the work itself motivating — achievement, responsibility, growth and recognition?
questions.why: Nothing above it will work. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Describe step 5 of the diagnosis sequence.
options: What am I reinforcing by what I notice and reward? Praise the behaviour you want; stop rewarding what you do not
Fix pay first, because nothing above a broken maintenance factor will work
Rewrite the objective in the textbook format with a measurable result and a date
Enrich the job so that the work itself provides achievement and growth
questions.why: Reinforcement step. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Explain the link between the diagnosis sequence and leader behaviour.
options: Steps 1–5 are mostly initiating structure; step 6 and the way you do all of them is consideration — the high-high leader does both
All steps are consideration, because motivation is about how the leader treats people
All steps are structure, because motivation is about goals, rewards and systems
The sequence replaces behaviour, because a leader who diagnoses correctly does not need a style
questions.why: Link to behaviour. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Identify which theory answers 'AED 250 each is forgotten in a month'.
options: Herzberg — a bonus is a maintenance factor; recognition and responsibility are motivators
Maslow — bonuses meet the self-actualisation need, which is never fully satisfied by any reward
Equity — the bonus is unfair because everyone received the same amount
Goal-setting — the bonus is vague because it was not tied to a specific goal
questions.why: Answer to question 3. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Exercise 1, leader A: the restaurant manager sets every table layout, times every order and never asks for ideas; turnover is high, the food is on time. Determine the Grid position and Ohio State style.
options: 9,1 authority-compliance — high structure, low consideration
1,9 country club — low structure, high consideration
9,9 team leader — high structure, high consideration, high commitment
1,1 impoverished — low structure, low consideration
questions.why: Answer key: A is 9,1. See §3.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1, leader B: the department head is loved by everyone, never gives hard feedback, and the unit misses most deadlines. Determine the Grid position.
options: 1,9 country club — low structure, high consideration
9,1 authority-compliance — high structure, low consideration
5,5 middle of the road — moderate structure, moderate consideration
9,9 team leader — high structure, high consideration
questions.why: Answer key: B is 1,9. See §3.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1, leader C: the site engineer agrees tough targets with the crew each morning, checks progress at noon and eats lunch with them — the safest, fastest site in the company. Determine the Grid position.
options: 9,9 team leader — high-high
9,1 authority-compliance — high structure, low consideration
5,5 middle of the road — moderate on both
1,9 country club — low structure, high consideration
questions.why: Answer key: C is 9,9. See §3.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1, leaders D and E: the supervisor who signs timesheets, avoids decisions and refers everything upward; and the call-centre leader with moderate targets, moderate feedback and average results. Determine their Grid positions.
options: D is 1,1 impoverished; E is 5,5 middle of the road
D is 5,5 middle of the road; E is 1,1 impoverished
Both are 9,1 authority-compliance
D is 1,9 country club; E is 9,9 team leader
questions.why: Answer key: D 1,1; E 5,5. See §3.3 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Analyse leader C's directive morning briefing inside a participative relationship. Determine why it does not damage commitment.
options: The targets are AGREED, so expectancy and goal acceptance stay high
Because engineers like orders and expect a site to be run by the person in charge
Because lunch is free, so the crew accepts the briefing as a fair exchange
Because the crane is new, so the crew is motivated by the equipment rather than the leader
questions.why: Answer key, task 3. See §3.2 and §3.6.

questions.stem: Classify the Iowa style of leader A (restaurant manager) and leader C (site engineer).
options: A is autocratic throughout; C uses a directive morning within a participative relationship
Both are democratic, because both set targets for the people who do the work
Both are autocratic, because both tell the team what to do each day
A is democratic because the food arrives on time; C is autocratic because he checks progress at noon
questions.why: Answer key, task 3. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Select ONE behaviour leader A should add to move toward 9,9, and the theory that predicts the effect.
options: Ask for ideas and give recognition — Herzberg's motivators, and equity through fairness
Raise everyone's pay — Maslow, because the restaurant staff are still at the physiological level
Add more rules — avoidance, so that staff work to avoid the manager's attention
Time orders more tightly — goal-setting, because tighter goals motivate more
questions.why: Answer key, task 2. See §3.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Select ONE behaviour leader B should add to move toward 9,9, and the theory.
options: Set specific deadlines with feedback and hold to them — goal-setting theory
Bake more cakes for the team — Maslow, because belongingness needs are unmet
Supervise less — Michigan, because employee-centred leaders should not check work
Pay a bonus for meeting deadlines — Herzberg, because bonuses are motivators
questions.why: Answer key, task 2. See §3.6 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, the delivery hub: salaries are paid on time but are the lowest of the three apps in the area. Determine the diagnosis-step finding and the theory.
options: Step 1 — a maintenance factor is partly unmet (Maslow/Herzberg): on time, but lowest pay
Step 4 — goal-setting: the pay target is not specific enough
Step 5 — reinforcement: pay is a positive reinforcer that is working
Step 6 — motivators: pay is the motivator the riders care about most, so growth comes second
questions.why: Marking guide, task 1: maintenance — lowest pay but on time (partial). See §3.8 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: the daily target of 45 deliveries is met by only a third of riders and the bonus is paid two months late. Determine the theory and the broken parts.
options: Expectancy theory — expectancy is low (target reachable by few) and instrumentality is broken (bonus paid late)
Equity theory — riders compare their inputs and outputs with the other two apps
Maslow — the safety need is unmet because the bonus is uncertain
Reinforcement — the late bonus is a punishment for slow riders
questions.why: Marking guide: expectancy low, instrumentality broken. See §3.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: riders say the fastest rider gets the best routes 'because the leader likes him'. Determine the theory and the finding.
options: Equity theory — route favouritism; perceived inequity lowers effort
Expectancy theory — valence is low because riders do not value good routes
Goal-setting — there is no feedback on which routes are best
Herzberg — pay is low, so routes do not matter
questions.why: Marking guide: equity — route favouritism. See §3.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: nobody has been thanked in months — Rashid only messages when a delivery is late. Determine what his behaviour is teaching the riders.
options: Accidental extinction of good work and an avoidance culture — only lateness gets attention
Positive reinforcement of speed, because the fastest riders are left alone and never messaged
Punishment of lateness only, which is the correct use of reinforcement
Goal acceptance, because riders know exactly what the leader expects
questions.why: Marking guide: reinforcement — only lateness gets attention. See §3.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: the work is repetitive and riders see no path to becoming a dispatcher. Determine the theory and the finding.
options: Herzberg's motivators / McClelland — no growth path; the work itself is not motivating
Equity theory — the routes are unfair so riders see no future
Maslow — the physiological need is unmet because the work is tiring
Expectancy theory — valence is zero because riders do not want to become dispatchers in the first place
questions.why: Marking guide: motivators — no growth path. See §3.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select the objective, in the textbook format, that repairs the hub's expectancy and goal-setting problems.
options: To raise the share of riders completing 40 deliveries a day from 33% to 70% by 31 March, with weekly feedback
Improve rider performance across the hub so that more riders reach the daily target more often
Riders should try to deliver more each day and the hub will do its best to support them
To be the best delivery hub in Sharjah by the end of the year, as measured by customer ratings and rider satisfaction scores
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §3.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select Rashid's reinforcement plan from the marking guide.
options: Recognise target-hitters weekly on a variable schedule, publish route rules, open a dispatcher pathway
Fine every late rider so that lateness falls quickly and the hub's customer rating recovers before the quarter ends
Pay a fixed annual bonus so that every rider knows exactly what to expect
Ignore everything except lateness, because lateness is what customers notice
questions.why: Marking guide, task 3. See §3.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Rashid praises the next rider who hits the target. Select the four-step praise.
options: 'Ali, you completed 45 on time today in the rain. That is what keeps our rating above 4.8.' (pause) 'Do it again tomorrow and I'll be watching.'
'Good job, Ali. Keep it up and we will see what we can do about the routes next week when the schedule is published.'
'Ali, you were late twice last week, but today was fine, so let's make sure this is the start of a much better pattern for you and for the whole team.'
'Everyone, well done today — the numbers were good and the customers were happy, so let's do the same again tomorrow.'
questions.why: Four steps: what, why, pause, encourage. See §3.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine where Rashid is on the Grid today and the two behaviours that move him toward 9,9.
options: 9,1 or 1,1 today; add consideration behaviours (thanks, fairness, growth) while keeping structure (clear targets)
9,9 already, because the targets are clear and the riders are paid on time
1,9 country club — add more targets and tighter supervision
5,5 middle of the road — change nothing, because the results are average
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4. See §3.3 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Analyse Rashid's situation. Determine why fixing recognition before the late bonus would fail.
options: Step 1–2 come first — a broken maintenance factor and broken instrumentality make everything above them fail
Recognition is unethical when pay is low, because it substitutes words for money
Riders dislike praise and would see it as manipulation
Bonuses are motivators, so they must come before recognition
questions.why: Fix it first; nothing above it will work. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Take-away: a student praises a team-mate with 'good job' and moves on. Determine what is missing from the four steps.
options: Step 1 — exactly what was done correctly — and the why, the pause and the encouragement
Nothing is missing — 'good job' is praise, and praise is exactly what the four steps are designed to produce
Only the pause, because the other three steps are implied by 'good job'
Only a reward, because praise without a bonus is incomplete
questions.why: Step 1 — specific, not 'good job'. See §3.7 and the take-away.

questions.stem: Take-away: the praise felt awkward and the student wanted to rush past the pause. Determine why the chapter insists on the pause.
options: Stop for a moment of silence — let it land; it is the step most managers skip
The pause is for the manager to think of what to say next
The pause is optional and can be skipped whenever the manager is short of time
The pause replaces step 2, because silence says why it matters
questions.why: Step 3. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Rami tells the team 'reach the fortress by dawn or we fail' though it is forty kilometres away over the pass. Determine the motivation effect.
options: Expectancy falls to zero — an impossible target demotivates
Goal-setting motivates — the target is specific and has a deadline
Equity rises, because everyone faces the same impossible target
Maintenance factors improve, because the team has a clear direction
questions.why: Impossible targets destroy expectancy. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Dana shivers all night with no blanket while Rami praises her tracking skills. Determine why the praise does not land.
options: A lower unmet need (physiological/safety) must be met first — a late salary cancels every award
Praise never works with followers who are tired
Dana lacks dominance and does not respond to recognition
Praise is a maintenance factor and does not motivate
questions.why: Find the lowest unmet need and meet it. See §3.5.

questions.stem: Noor's clever idea at the camp is ignored; the next day she stops offering ideas. Classify what happened.
options: Extinction — the unrewarded behaviour faded
Punishment — Noor was penalised for speaking
Positive reinforcement — Noor was rewarded for silence
Avoidance — Noor is behaving to avoid criticism
questions.why: Good work going unnoticed. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Analyse the river crossing: Rami gives direct orders, assigns ropes and checks every knot himself. Determine whether this is the right Iowa style.
options: Yes — autocratic style fits emergencies and unskilled or new followers
No — democratic is always better, because it builds commitment
No — he should vote on who takes which rope
No — he should step back and let the team organise the crossing for itself as it sees fit
questions.why: Works with emergencies and new staff. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Omar carried the heaviest pack all week; Dana carried nothing and got the same share of food. Determine the theory and the likely behaviour.
options: Equity theory — under-rewarded, Omar will reduce effort or demand change
Expectancy theory — valence is low because Omar does not value the extra food he would receive
Goal-setting — Omar has no feedback on his carrying
Herzberg — food is a maintenance factor and does not motivate
questions.why: Perceived inequity changes behaviour. See §3.6.

questions.stem: Classify Rami, who sets clear tasks for the climb AND checks how each follower feels before they start.
options: Ohio State high-high — high initiating structure and high consideration
Michigan job-centred only — the tasks matter more than the people
Michigan employee-centred only — the feelings matter more than the tasks
Low-low abdication — Rami is leaving the climb to the team
questions.why: Both at once. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Rami rewards Omar's scouting at unpredictable moments rather than every evening. Determine the schedule and why it works.
options: Variable intermittent schedule — produces the most durable behaviour
Continuous schedule — best for everything because every good act is rewarded
Punishment — stops the behaviour that is not rewarded
Fixed schedule — stops motivating once it becomes predictable
questions.why: Unpredictable recognition works. See §3.7.

questions.stem: Analyse Dana, who works hard for a week, is thanked, and then wants a bigger role. Determine the stage of the motivation process this shows.
options: Satisfaction — the need is met and a new one appears
Need only — Dana has not yet acted on it
Consequence only — Dana has been thanked
Dissatisfaction — Dana wanted a bigger role from the start
questions.why: The cycle continues. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Identify step 6 of the diagnosis sequence.
options: Is the work itself motivating — achievement, responsibility, growth? Enrich the job; delegate; recognise
Fix pay first, because a broken maintenance factor cancels everything above it
Rewrite the objective in the textbook format so that it is measurable
Explain the differences in pay and routes to every rider so that they are understood and seen as fair by all
questions.why: Herzberg motivators and McClelland. See §3.8.

questions.stem: Noor asks the team how to cross the marsh, listens, and lets them choose the path; the next day they cross without her. Classify the Iowa style and its effect.
options: Democratic — commitment and effort that continues without the leader
Autocratic — dependence on the leader for every decision the team faces
Laissez-faire — abandonment of the team to its own devices
Transactional — an exchange of effort for reward
questions.why: Democratic style produces effort that continues without the leader. See §3.1.

questions.stem: The Crow chief decides everything and his guards stop working the moment he leaves the courtyard. Classify the style and the chapter's warning.
options: Autocratic — effort falls when the leader leaves the room
Democratic — commitment that lasts after the leader leaves
High-high — the ideal combination of structure and consideration
Country club — pleasant for the guards but weak on results
questions.why: Produces dependence. See §3.1.

questions.stem: Classify Dana, who is warm with everyone but never sets a task or checks a result.
options: Low initiating structure, high consideration
High initiating structure, low consideration
High initiating structure, high consideration
Low initiating structure, low consideration
questions.why: Ohio State four styles. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Classify the Crow chief, who sets strict tasks, checks everything and never asks how his men feel.
options: High initiating structure, low consideration
High initiating structure, high consideration
Low initiating structure, high consideration
Low initiating structure, low consideration
questions.why: Task-focused; results now, morale later. See §3.2.

questions.stem: Omar wants recognition, so he scouts harder, Rami thanks him publicly, and Omar is satisfied — then wants a bigger role. Determine the process illustrated.
options: Need → motive → behaviour → consequence → satisfaction, and a new need appears
Equity theory — Omar compares the recognition he receives with what Dana receives
Reinforcement schedule — Rami is rewarding on a variable basis
Goal-setting — Omar has a specific goal and feedback
questions.why: The motivation process. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Determine which class of theory answers 'why is Dana not trying, although she knows the goal?'.
options: Process theories — how people choose behaviour
Content theories — which needs motivate
Reinforcement theory — what consequences teach
Trait theory — what kind of person Dana is
questions.why: Process: why the person is not trying. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Determine which class of theory answers 'what is Rami's own behaviour teaching the team?'.
options: Reinforcement theory
Content theories
Process theories
Behavioural theories
questions.why: Reinforcement: what your responses teach. See §3.4.

questions.stem: Rami gives Noor a hard navigation puzzle with daily feedback, Omar the responsibility for the camp, and Dana a role in the group songs. Determine the theory applied.
options: McClelland's acquired needs — challenge for achievers, responsibility for power-seekers, teamwork for affiliators
Maslow — all three followers are at the same level of the hierarchy
Herzberg — all three tasks are maintenance factors
Equity theory — all three followers receive the same treatment
questions.why: Leader's use of acquired needs. See §3.5.

questions.stem: The team's pay is fine and the goal is clear, but Omar believes effort will not be rewarded because Rami broke his last promise. Determine the diagnosis step and the fix.
options: Step 2 — expectancy: reliable rewards and promises kept
Step 1 — fix pay, because the team's pay is the real problem
Step 4 — rewrite the goal so that it is more specific
Step 6 — enrich the job so that Omar finds the work itself motivating
questions.why: Does the person believe effort → performance → reward? See §3.8.

questions.stem: Determine the correct order for Rami to use the theories, according to the chapter.
options: Basics, expectancy, equity, goals, reinforcement, motivators
Motivators first, then pay once the team is engaged
Goals first, then basics once the goals are accepted
Reinforcement only, because what the leader rewards is what gets done
questions.why: A leader's diagnosis sequence. See §3.8.
